id: The Zebra Goes Wild Where the Sidewalk Ends

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I Neon stripes tighten my wall where my crayon landlord hangs from a bent nail. My black father sits crooked in the kitchen drunk on Jesus’ blood turned to cheap wine. In his tremor he curses the landlord who grins from inside the rent book. My father’s eyes are bolls of cotton. He sits upon the landlord’s operating table, the needle of the nation sucking his soul. II Chains of light race over my stricken city. Glittering web spun by the white widow spider. I see this wild arena where we are harnessed by alien electric shadows. Even when the sun washes the debris I will recall my landlord hanging in my room and my father moaning in Jesus’ tomb. In America all zebras are in the zoo. I hear the piston bark and ibm spark: let us program rabies. the madness is foaming now. No wild zebras roam the American plain. The mad dogs are running. The African zebra is gone into the dust. I see the shadow thieves coming and my father on the specimen table.

- The speaker describes a childhood home where a crayon-drawn landlord hangs on the wall, symbolizing the oppressive presence of financial exploitation in domestic life.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem depicts a Black father's degradation and suffering under systemic oppression, using surreal imagery of a "crayon landlord," alcoholism, and mechanized violence to portray exploitation and dehumanization, while the speaker witnesses this decay within a technologically alienating American landscape. The extended metaphor of zebras confined to zoos and vanishing into "dust" reveals the poem's central significance: America has systematically erased and contained Black wildness/freedom, reducing living beings to specimens under clinical, inhuman control.

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your piece, refined for eloquence and flow while preserving every image, symbol, and meaning from the original:

---

**I**

Neon stripes constrict my walls, where my crayon-rendered landlord hangs from a bent nail. My black father slumps crookedly in the kitchen, drunk on Jesus' blood transmuted into cheap wine. Trembling, he curses the landlord who grins from within the pages of the rent book. My father's eyes have become bolls of cotton. He lies upon the landlord's operating table, while the nation's needle draws the soul from him.

**II**

Chains of light race across my stricken city—a glittering web spun by the white widow spider. I witness this savage arena where we are harnessed beneath alien, electric shadows. Even when dawn's light washes over the debris, I will remember my landlord hanging in my room, and my father moaning in Jesus' tomb.

In America, all zebras are confined to the zoo. I hear the piston bark and the IBM spark: *let us program rabies*. The madness now foams at the mouth. No wild zebra roams the American plain. The mad dogs are loose. The African zebra has vanished into dust. I see the shadow-thieves approaching, and my father lies upon the specimen table.

---

I've smoothed transitions, sharpened parallel structures (e.g., "let us program rabies" as an italicized, ominous command), and refined word choices like "constrict," "transmuted," and "savage arena" to heighten the poem's visceral, prophetic tone—while keeping every original image, symbol, and narrative beat intact. Let me know if you'd like a version with different stylistic emphasis (more clipped/urgent, or more lyrical/flowing).
outputs.L2:
**I.**

Fluorescent bands cinch my wall tight, where the crayon drawing of my landlord dangles from a crooked nail. My Black father slumps sideways in the kitchen, intoxicated on what was once Jesus' blood, now reduced to bargain wine. Shaking, he damns the landlord who smirks at him from the pages of the rent ledger. My father's eyes have become tufts of raw cotton. He is stretched across the landlord's surgical table, while the nation's needle drains his very spirit.

**II.**

Ribbons of light streak across my wounded city—a shimmering net woven by the pale widow spider. I witness this savage coliseum where foreign electric shadows have us tethered and controlled. Even after sunlight clears away the wreckage, I will still remember my landlord's portrait swinging in my room, and my father groaning as if sealed inside Jesus' burial cave.

Here in America, every zebra lives behind zoo bars. I hear the engine's growl and IBM's electric hum: they're programming rabies into the system. The frenzy is already frothing over. No zebras run free across American fields anymore. The rabid dogs are loose now. The African zebra has vanished into dust and memory. I watch the shadow-stealers approaching, and my father lying on the examination table like a specimen.
outputs.L3:
# The Crayon Landlord: A Reading of Domestic Oppression and Systemic Violence

In this haunting piece of imagery-laden poetry, the speaker constructs a childhood memory that transcends simple nostalgia to become a searing indictment of systemic oppression. The poem opens with a striking domestic image: a crayon drawing of a landlord hanging on the wall of the family home. This is no innocent childhood artwork—it represents the way financial exploitation embeds itself into the very fabric of domestic life, becoming so omnipresent that even a child renders it in crayon, memorializing the landlord's oppressive presence as a fixture of home life itself. The landlord becomes an icon, almost religious in its constancy, watching over the family's poverty and precarity.

The father figure emerges as a central and tragic presence in this domestic tableau. Portrayed as a Black man struggling with alcoholism, he is not condemned but rather understood as a casualty of systemic suffering—a man broken not by personal failing but by the crushing weight of a society designed to grind him down. The poem employs striking religious imagery to underscore this degradation: Jesus' blood, the sacred symbol of salvation and sacrifice, is transformed into "cheap wine." This transubstantiation in reverse suggests that even the sacred has been debased and commodified within the father's world, that redemption itself has been cheapened and made accessible only through the numbing escape of alcohol. His drunkenness becomes not sin but symptom—evidence of a spirit worn down by forces far beyond his individual control.

This sense of the father as victim intensifies through the metaphor of the "operating table," where he becomes subject to experimentation, dissection, and consumption by "the needle of the nation." This is visceral, clinical imagery—suggesting that the father's body and spirit are being systematically probed, drained, and exploited by the machinery of the state itself. The needle suggests both medical intrusion and perhaps the track marks of addiction, conflating personal suffering with institutional violence, as if the nation itself is administering the poison that destroys him. He is not merely suffering; he is being actively consumed, his humanity extracted like a resource.

The poem then pivots to one of its most powerful metaphors: the zebra. In Africa, the zebra roams wild and free, embodying natural liberty and authentic identity. In America, however, this same creature exists only behind bars, confined to zoos for spectacle and containment. This transformation—from wild freedom to caged display—becomes a devastating metaphor for the Black experience in America, suggesting a fundamental displacement and loss of identity. The zebra, stripped of its natural context and freedom, becomes an object of curiosity rather than a living being with agency, much as the poem suggests Black Americans have been forced into a similar confinement, their essential nature caged by a society that reduces them to spectacle rather than recognizing their full humanity.

Finally, the poem broadens its critique to encompass technological and institutional forces, invoking IBM, mechanical pistons, and the chilling phrase "programmed rabies." These references suggest that oppression has evolved beyond simple physical confinement into something more insidious and pervasive—a systematic madness embedded in the very technologies and institutions that structure modern life. The reference to IBM suggests corporate and bureaucratic control, the reduction of human lives to data and systems. "Programmed rabies" is a particularly chilling phrase, suggesting that madness itself has become mechanized, intentional, and infectious—a designed dysfunction rather than organic disease. This is control that spreads like contagion, engineered by the same forces that built the operating tables and the cages, extending the poem's critique from the intimate space of the family home to the vast, impersonal machinery of the nation itself.

Together, these images build a cumulative portrait of systemic oppression that operates at every scale—from the personal and domestic to the institutional and technological—revealing how deeply dehumanization can penetrate, transforming even childhood memories into evidence of a nation's failures.
outputs.L4:
# Zebra Dust

My father comes home
speaking in the tongue of gears,
his hands stripped down to sprockets
by a crayon landlord
who colors outside every line
except the one that keeps him renting
his own skin back
from a system built to bill him
for existing.

The landlord's teeth are wax.
His smile melts under kitchen light,
dripping promises
that harden into debt.
He measures my father's worth
in fractions of a man,
in bottles emptied
like confession booths
where the only priest
is 80 proof forgiveness.

I watch my father
become a machine himself—
joints clicking like a assembly line,
voice flattening into static,
the television glow
replacing the sun
he used to walk beneath
before concrete swallowed the horizon
and turned every street
into a circuit board
wired for his failure.

At night I dream of zebras.
Not the ones in books,
but real ones, running—
black and white lightning
across some ancestral plain
that exists now only
in the space behind my eyelids.

In the zoo they call it habitat.
They call the bars *protection*,
the moat *conservation*,
as if freedom were a disease
that needed containing,
as if wildness itself
was something to be cured.

The zebras pace.
Their stripes blur
into a single gray smear
each time they pass
the same fake rock,
the same painted sky,
until even their pacing
becomes a kind of dust—
particles of what they were
before someone decided
their running needed watching,
their breathing needed metrics,
their bodies needed to become
educational specimens
behind glass that never once
asks permission
to turn a life
into a lesson.

My father was born running.
I have seen photographs—
his younger self,
unclipped, unbroken,
before the crayon landlord
before the wires
before America decided
that his kind of freedom
was a liability
to be managed,
a wildness
to be zoned,
a stripe pattern
too loud
for polite fences.

Now he sits in the blue static
of a screen that watches him
more than he watches it,
his laughter reduced
to something automated,
his rage reduced
to something they can medicate,
his love reduced
to something
they can litigate
in the fine print
of every lease
he never really signed
but was born already owing.

I want to tell him
the zebras are still out there—
somewhere past the enclosure,
past the moat,
past the crayon walls
melting in devouring light.

But I've seen the dust too.
I've seen how it settles
on everything that runs
long enough
in a space
too small
to hold it.

And I wonder
if freedom
is just another word
for the last thing
they let you keep
before they turn you
into an exhibit,
before the whole country
becomes a zoo
and every Black body
in it
just another
species
they've already
decided
is
going extinct.
outputs.L5:
# The Neon Cross

The bar's sign flickered red and blue against the wet pavement, a neon Jesus figure hanging above the door—arms outstretched, glowing softly in the misty evening air. It was an odd choice for a dive bar called "Redemption," but the owner, Mack, had always had a strange sense of humor about his establishment.

Inside, chains hung from the ceiling like industrial vines, remnants from the building's days as a warehouse. They swayed slightly whenever someone opened the door, catching the neon glow and scattering fractured light across the bar. Regular patrons barely noticed them anymore, but newcomers often stared upward, unsettled by the juxtaposition—chains and salvation, bondage and light.

Sarah sat at the corner stool, watching the neon Jesus buzz and hum through the window. She'd been coming here for three months now, ever since she'd broken free from something she still couldn't quite name. A relationship, a pattern, a version of herself that had felt like iron links wrapped around her ribs.

"Another one?" Mack asked, wiping down the bar.

She nodded, glancing again at the neon glow bleeding through the glass. There was something comforting about it—gaudy and sacred all at once, buzzing with electricity instead of divine light, but present nonetheless. A reminder that even manufactured grace could illuminate a dark corner.

The chains above her creaked as the door opened, someone new stepping in from the rain, chasing warmth, chasing whatever it was that drew broken people toward flickering signs and quiet corners.

Outside, the neon Jesus kept watch, arms open, indifferent to the weather, indifferent to time—just glowing, steady and strange, for anyone who needed to look up.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, angry poem about growing up Black in America, using imagery of a landlord, a drunk father, and animals like zebras to symbolize oppression.
counterfactuals.output:
# Inheritance

The landlord of my skin collects rent
in the currency of my grandmother's knees,
bent so long they forgot
how straight feels.
He never shows his face,
only leaves notices nailed to my chest:
*past due, past due, past due*—
as if I hadn't been paying
since before I had hands.

My father drinks the color of dusk
from a bottle shaped like a noose,
loosening his tongue into thunder,
and I learn early
that love can arrive
with its knuckles first,
that some men pour their cages
into glasses
and call it medicine.

I dream of zebras some nights—
not the black, not the white,
but the *bars themselves*,
walking upright, grazing
on a savanna that keeps shrinking
into a parking lot,
into a projects courtyard,
into the six-by-eight cell
of a body that was never
allowed to just be flesh.

The zebras ask me: *which stripe are you tonight?*
I say I am tired of being asked
to choose a color
for a war I did not start,
a war stitched into my birth certificate,
a war the landlord charges extra for.

America, you drunk father,
you absent architecture of promises—
you built your house on my spine
and called the crookedness *character*.
You handed me a mirror
made of prison bars
and told me to smile
for the family photo.

I am the rent that's never paid off.
I am the zebra with no herd,
striped by hands that aren't my own,
grazing on a country
that keeps eating its own children
and calling it *breakfast*,
calling it *tradition*,
calling it, God help us,
*home*.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a two-part free verse poem in the style of Amiri Baraka or the Black Arts Movement, blending religious imagery, poverty, and technological control.
counterfactuals.output:
# Electric Testament

## I. The Body Bears Witness

Grandmama's Bible got a cellphone charger
tucked in Exodus, right where Moses
lift his rod against the water—

we drowning too, but slower,
in the blue light of screens that watch us
sleep, that count our footsteps
like Judas counting silver,
thirty pieces for a soul,
now it's free, now it's *terms and conditions*,
now it's *accept to continue*—

I seen God in the rent notice,
red ink like the blood on the doorframe
but ain't no angel passing over this house,
just the landlord's algorithm,
calculating who gets to eat
based on credit scores
written by the same hands
that wrote *Whereas* and *hereby*
into the Constitution
while we were three-fifths
of a download, buffering
still, three-fifths of a citizen
in a nation of full pixels—

Jesus wept, the shortest verse,
but they don't teach the one where
he flips tables in the market,
where he say *blessed are the poor*
and mean it as diagnosis, not destiny.

## II. Surveillance of the Spirit

They put a camera on the corner
where the church used to be loud
with tambourines and testimony,
now it just watches, unblinking,
recording who loiters near the promise
of a store that don't cash our checks
without two forms of ID
and a reason to exist—

Mama said *the eye of God sees all*
but she ain't know they'd patent it,
sell it back to us in monthly installments,
call it *safety*, call it *protection*,
same word they used for the overseer,
same word stamped on the drone
that hover like a false Pentecost—
no tongues of fire, just static,
just the hum of something deciding
whether we're a threat
or just background noise
in somebody else's American dream,

and still—
still we sing.
Still the choir robes hang
pressed and ready in closets
that smell like mothballs and hope,
still we find the beat
in the malfunction,
still we make manna
out of what the system
meant to starve us with—

data mining our neighborhoods
for patterns of "risk"
while we mine the psalms
for patterns of resurrection,
because we've done this before—
turned tracking devices into testimony,
turned chains into rhythm,
turned the whole machinery of control
into something that still, somehow,
sounds like freedom
when we sing it loud enough
to wake the dead,
loud enough
to short the circuit,
loud enough
to make the cameras blink first.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark, symbolic poem about a father's suffering under systemic racism, incorporating images of chains, zoos, and corporate machinery like IBM.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ledger of a Man

They filed him under a number,
punched his name into a card,
IBM teeth chewing through
the meat of his hours—
each hole a small mouth
screaming what he could not say
in the break room, in the boardroom,
in the fluorescent hum
where his shadow was measured
but never his height.

At home he was a father.
At work he was a metric,
a productivity chain
link by link by link,
forged not of iron now
but of quotas and quiet,
of doors that opened
onto smaller and smaller rooms.

I remember the zoo we visited once—
how the lion paced his allotted grass,
eyes flat as August pavement,
dignity folded into a shape
that fit the enclosure.
My father watched longer than I did.
Didn't say why.
Didn't have to.

Some cages don't need bars.
Some chains are made of paperwork,
of *not quite qualified*,
of smiling supervisors
who never learned his first name
but knew his employee ID
by heart.

He came home smelling of copier toner
and swallowed rage,
sat at the table like a monument
to some war with no medals,
no name carved anywhere
but in the lines of his face,
in the silence he wore
like a second uniform.

I used to think strength
was the absence of breaking.
Now I know
it's the daily art
of not shattering
in front of your children—

of taking the chain,
coiling it quietly,
and calling it
a belt,
calling it
enough.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental poem exploring themes of exploitation and loss of freedom, using the metaphor of caged zebras and a predatory landlord in an urban Black household.
counterfactuals.output:
**stripes / stripped**

i.

Mama says we come from stripes—
              black         white         black         white
                    running like fence posts down our backs,
        like the bars on the security door
                    Mr. Kaminsky installed
              after the third break-in
        that wasn't ever us.

She says *baby, a zebra's stripes
        are a cage it wears on the outside
              so the cage on the inside
                    don't show.*

ii.

RENT DUE THE 1ST
        (no grace, no mercy, no minute)
              RENT DUE THE 1ST
        the landlord circles our building
              like something with teeth,
        calls it "checking on his property"
              like we the deer
                    like we the stock
              like we the exhibit
        behind glass he don't clean.

iii.

              stripe / strip
        strip / stripped
              stripped of— 

*heat*
        (he says the boiler's "temperamental")
*hot water*
        (he says "next Tuesday" for the ninth Tuesday)
*the lease we asked to see in writing*
        (he says "trust me")

trust
        is a zoo word.
              trust is what they call it
        when the fence
              is far enough away
                    you forget
              it's a fence.

iv.

Grandma kept a zebra figurine
        on the windowsill,
              painted wood, chipped mane,
        said her grandmother carried one
              wrapped in a headscarf
                    through customs, through Ellis,
              through the actual ocean—
        said *we have always
              been beautiful
                    and hunted
              at the same damn time.*

v.

              in the dream i am grazing
        in the dream there is no roof
              only savanna-colored ceiling stains
        shaped like a country
              i cannot pronounce

in the dream the landlord is a lion
        but slower than the myths say,
              he only wins
        because the grass
              agreed to lie down first—

              i wake up
        and the grass is my mother's back
                    bent over the stove
              cooking dinner at 9 p.m.
        because the shift ran long
              because the bus ran late
        because the fence
              runs everywhere
                    she runs.

vi.

              stripe             cage
        stripe             cage
              stripe             cage

we learned to read the pattern
        before we learned to read—
              knew which knock meant *rent*
        knew which knock meant *inspection*
              knew which knock
                    would never come
        because some doors
              he doesn't bother knocking,
                    just enters,
              because a body in a cage
        is a body he already paid for,
              (he thinks),
                    already owns the right
              to walk into.

vii.

but a zebra, cornered,
        will kick.
              will break a jaw
        will run itself bloody
              rather than lie down
                    for anybody's fence.

so here:
        my mother's name on every lease she's ever signed
              in her own handwriting, not his—
        my grandmother's figurine
              still on the sill, un-sold, un-hocked—
        my own two hands
              learning the word *tenant*
        learning the word *rights*
              learning that the stripe
        is not the whole animal,
              is only the shadow
                    the cage throws
              when the light hits wrong—

and underneath the shadow:
        muscle.
              hoof.
        a body that remembers
              how to run
                    toward something
              instead of only
        away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a raw, stream-of-consciousness poem about generational trauma, alcoholism, and systemic control, filled with vivid, nightmarish imagery of America as a cage.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Bottle Remembers

my grandfather's hands shook before mine did
learned it from his father who learned it from a war
that learned it from a flag that learned it from a noose
this is how the poison travels—
not through blood but through silence,
through Sunday dinners where nobody asks
why Daddy's eyes go glassy at 4pm
why Mama flinches at car doors slamming
why the belt hangs on that nail like it's decoration
like it's not a threat wearing the shape of discipline

America you raised me on channel surf and static prayer
told me I was free while measuring my throat for the collar
told me pull yourself up while cutting off my hands
told me land of opportunity
while the opportunity was always
someone else's boot on someone else's neck
someone else's grandfather's grandfather's chains
rebranded as bootstraps

I'm drinking my dead men's medicine
straight from the bottle labeled Fine, I'm Fine
labeled This Is Normal
labeled Everyone's Family Is Like This, Right?

the cage doesn't look like bars here
it looks like a mortgage
looks like minimum wage and a hospital bill
that costs more than the surgery saved
looks like a badge and a knee
looks like my uncle's DUI mugshot
next to the senator's DUI dismissal

we are all just repeating the seance
calling up ghosts we never buried right
Daddy drank to forget what his daddy did to him
I drink to forget I remember
my kids will drink to forget the forgetting

the flag doesn't wave, it strangles—
red for the blood we pretend is paint
white for the lie we tell about purity
blue for the bruises we call patriotism

I dreamed last night the whole country
was one long hallway of locked doors
and behind every door was my father
crying in a way I never saw when he was alive
and behind every door was me
crying in a way I never let anyone see
and behind every door was America
selling the key
back to us
at market price

somebody tell me how to stop
the inheritance
somebody tell me how to break
the chain without breaking my own hand
somebody tell me freedom isn't just
a bigger cage
with a flag flying
over the bars

I'm not drunk
I'm just remembering
everything
they built this whole country
to help me
forget
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
